newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak crown seen firmer despite profit-taking.
newsitem.headline: Slovak crown seen firmer despite profit-taking.

text.p: The Slovak crown, bolstered in recent days by a sudden inflow of foreign funds, should continue to strengthen despite a round of profit-taking that has slowed its progress, analysts said on Tuesday.

The crown flirted with its mark/dollar basket parity level on Monday, rising more than one full percentage point against the dollar, as investors were attracted by rising interest rates spurred by central bank measures to tighten liquidity.
Despite a round of profit-taking that eroded some 20 basis points from its gains early on Tuesday, dealers said they expected the currency to rise further.
"The crown may rise to above parity even today, despite moving in the opposite direction at the moment," Vladimir Akubzanov, a VUB Bank forex dealer, told Reuters.

The crown was trading at 32.252 to the dollar and 19.889 against the mark in the early afternoon, putting it 0.33 percent below parity with the mark/dollar basket which the National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) uses to fix the currency daily.
Dealers estimated that some $80 million of last week's inflow of $150-200 million had been pulled from the market over the past two days.

Stronger crown sales also prompted the NBS to interrupt a series of stronger crown fixes. On Tuesday it fixed the crown at 0.50 percent below the basket midpoint, after fixing it at 0.30 percent below on Monday, and 1.84 percent below a week ago.

"The parity has triggered profit-taking, dampening the crown. But we are in the correction stage only. The trend will reverse and we will certainly see a new inflow in the foreseeable future," said Peter Koprna of Slovenska Sporitelna.
"I see a very strong resistance at 0.55-0.60 percent below parity."

The banking sector became highly illiquid after the NBS stopped quoting securities repurchase and reverse repurchase rates at the start of the year, instead holding tenders when needed for limited volumes of short-term securities repos.

The move, which pushed interest rates to near record levels last week before they retreated slightly, is the latest by the NBS to rein in a rapidly growing money supply and cool off a consumption-led economic boom.

At the same time, the NBS set new rules at the beginning of the year for foreign exchange positions for monetary purposes -- and penalties for breaching the measures -- in an attempt to reduce the sector's rapid loan expansion.

But dealers said some banks had begun to adjust deposit rates to foreign clients to offset the costs of the central bank move and attract liquidity, although they warned the inflows have receded as rates ease.

"One has to consider that the number of those reopening or opening positions lessens, I rather expect withdrawals once the crown climbs over the midpoint," Brano Matusek, a dealer at Tatra Banka, told Reuters.
ING Bank money market dealer Rastislav Zivor added: "There are enough crowns in the (banking) sector, but no interbank credit lines to allow their redistribution."
Short-term interest rates had fallen an average 100 basis points to the 18-19 percent level on Tuesday.
